newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka troops dig in after taking rebel town.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka troops dig in after taking rebel town.

text.p: Sri Lankan troops were consolidating positions on Friday, the fourth day of an offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels, after taking a northern rebel-held town, military officials said.

Military officials in the north of the Indian Ocean island told Reuters that police reinforcements had been sent to the town, Omanthai, north of the government-held town of Vavuniya, to help the army secure the newly-captured territory.

Troops, backed by artillery, tanks and helicopter gunships, broke out of their bases in Vavuniya, 220 km (135 miles) north of Colombo, on Tuesday, launching an offensive code-named "Jaya Sikuru", or "Sure of Victory", into the rebel-held northern Wanni heartland.
"Overnight there was no confrontation" with the rebel Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), a military spokesman in Colombo told Reuters on Friday.
LTTE transmissions monitored by the army on Thursday said at least 100 rebels had been killed or wounded in the battle for Omanthai, a Defence Ministry spokesman said.
Army casualties in Omanthai and elsewhere stood at 18 dead and 31 wounded in the four-day-old offensive, he said.

The LTTE are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east. The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
The clandestine rebel Voice of Tiger radio, monitored in Vavuniya, said on Friday that the LTTE had put up stiff resistance at Omanthai to stop the troops' advance.
Residents in Vavuniya said shelling was continuing from military bases there on LTTE positions in the Wanni, the large swathe of northern rebel-controlled jungle territory.
They said air force planes had also been seen flying towards Wanni from a base at the ancient Sri Lankan capital of Anuradhapura, 50 km (30 miles) south of Vavuniya.
On Thursday, troops advancing from the northern frontline town of Puvarasankulam met stiff resistance from the LTTE at Kuruvikulam, west of Vavuniya, military officials said.
A military official said at least 12 rebels were killed and more were believed wounded in the Kuruvikulam battle. The number of army casualties was not known, he added.

Analysts said the aim of the fresh offensive was to open a land supply route linking Vavuniya with the Jaffna peninsula, about 100 km (60 miles) further north. Jaffna town, the capital of the rebels' wouldbe homeland, is under government control.
But the military has been tight-lipped about where the troops are heading.
The LTTE's international spokesman in London accused the military on Thursday of killing Tamil civilians and destroying their property under the guise of opening up a supply route.
"Army artillery has been raining down on Tamil civilians and on their homes and in most cases they were nowhere near the supply route the army wants to open," Anton Raja told Reuters by telephone.
He said droves of civilians have abandoned their homes to seek shelter in the mosquito-infested jungle.
An international aid worker in Vavuniya told Reuters at least 10 civilians had been killed and more wounded in the artillery shelling of the Wanni.

Other aid workers said they had not seen large-scale civilian movement as witnessed during previous offensives. A large number, anticipating Tuesday's offensive, had already moved to safer locations, they said.
